newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam, China move closer on maritime row talks.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam, China move closer on maritime row talks.

text.p: Vietnam said on Wednesday that China had proposed holding expert-level talks next week on competing claims to a potentially gas-rich area between Hainan island and Vietnam's central coast.

"We have asked for discussions between experts as soon as possible," Foreign Minister Nguyen Manh Cam told reporters after the opening of the National Assembly's spring session. "China has proposed next week."
He said the venue for negotiations still had to be discussed, but Vietnamese officials were ready to visit Beijing if the suggestion of meeting in Hanoi was not accepted.
Chinese officials said on Tuesday that Beijing was preparing for talks on the dispute.

An official of China's main offshore oil firm said the talks would focus on sovereignty of an area 64.5 nautical miles off the Vietnamese coast where exploratory drilling by a Chinese rig has sparked verbal sparring between the communist neighbours.
"The talks will focus on the division of the sea and will discuss who owns that continental shelf and economic region," he said.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang said bilateral disputes over territory and resource exploration in the South China Sea could be resolved through peaceful and friendly consultations.
That was echoed on Wednesday by Do Muoi, Secretary General of Vietnam's Communist Party, who told reporters he believed both sides had the goodwill to settle the problem and preserve peace.
Asked why Hanoi had protested so publicly to Beijing if China had been drilling in that area for the past four years, he said there was a time for both quiet and outspoken diplomacy.
Hanoi has repeatedly demanded that China withdraw the rig and support vessels from the area and has presented its case to fellow members of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN).
However, only one of the seven ASEAN countries -- the Philippines -- has publicly backed Vietnam's position. Others have said they see the dispute as a bilateral issue.

Officials of the China National Offshore Oil Corp, which already oversees exploitation of lucrative gas fields off the southern island province of Hainan, said last week that they had no immediate plans to move the rig.
"Why should we leave the area?" one official said. "When the exploration is finished we will move the rig."
The exploration row is the latest in a long series of territorial disputes, ideological differences and historical grievances to strain Sino-Vietnamese socialist solidarity.
The two nations have competing claims on areas along their land border, on parts of the Tonkin Gulf and on the Paracel Islands, which lie east of the latest area of dispute.
They are also among six regional claimants to the Spratly islands further to the south.

Both sides have in recent years agreed to shelve some border problems and have worked hard to improve ties and boost border trade. But the temptation to exploit the oil- and gas-rich waters they dispute has been a constant threat to their rapprochement.
